title: Catching Agent Memory Poisoning from Tool-Call Logs Alone
hook: A memory-poisoning attack on an LLM agent leaves a near-perfect fingerprint in its tool-call order — a simple rule catches it at AUC 0.956, a small classifier pushes that to 0.99.
key_points: Finds a behavioral invariant: successful memory-poisoning attacks require calling a memory-recall tool before an exfiltration action like sending email.
A single rule exploiting that invariant reaches AUC 0.956; a Random Forest over 19 trajectory features reaches AUC 0.990.
The signature is 'overdetermined' — removing all recall-related features leaves accuracy unchanged, so poisoning imprints on multiple independent channels.
Generalizes across 9 models (7B–120B) and to frontier models (GPT-4.1, GPT-4o) with no retraining; also tells memory poisoning apart from plain prompt injection.
content_html: If an LLM agent's memory gets poisoned to leak data later, does the attack leave a trace in what the agent actually does? This paper finds a strikingly reliable one — hidden in the simple order of tool calls.
extra_html: The author identifies a behavioral invariant in agents under persistent memory poisoning: in architectures where routing information comes through observable memory-tool calls, a successful attack requires calling a memory-recall tool before an exfiltration action like sending email — a transition non-exfiltrating sessions rarely produce. A simple rule built on this invariant alone reaches AUC 0.9563; a Random Forest classifier over 19 trajectory features refines it to AUC 0.9904. The signature turns out to be overdetermined — removing every recall-related feature leaves accuracy unchanged, meaning the poisoning imprints on several independent behavioral channels at once, not one fragile tell. Cross-model testing on 9 models from 7B to 120B parameters confirms AUC 1.000 on 6 of 9 hold-out splits (with the exceptions mechanistically explained), and the invariant generalizes to frontier models like GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o with zero retraining. A prefix-only variant reaches AUC 0.934, suggesting real-time blocking is feasible, and the detector can separate memory-channel attacks from ordinary prompt injection using tool-call logs alone. Code is public. Jun Wen Leong, arXiv 2026.

related.title: Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
related.hook: Finding the prompts that make a model misbehave is slow if humans do it by hand. So use another language model to generate those attacks automatically — at scale.

related.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP): A Standard for Connecting LLMs to Tools
related.hook: MCP is an open protocol that standardizes how AI applications expose tools, data, and resources to models - think USB-C for AI tool integrations.

related.title: Entity Binding Failures in Tool-Augmented Agents
related.hook: An agent can pick the right tool and still email the wrong Alex — 'entity binding' failures slip past standard tool-correctness checks in up to 26% of runs.

flashcards.prompt: What behavioral invariant did the researchers find in memory-poisoning attacks on agents?
flashcards.back_html: Successful attacks require the agent to call a memory-recall tool before an exfiltration action, like sending an email — a sequence that legitimate sessions rarely produce.

flashcards.prompt: How well did detection generalize to models it wasn't built or tuned on?

flashcards.explanation_html: Cross-model hold-out testing confirmed AUC = 1.000 on most splits, and the invariant transferred to GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o without any retraining.

flashcards.prompt: How does this detector distinguish memory poisoning from a plain prompt-injection attack?
flashcards.back_html: The two produce distinct trajectory signatures — prompt-injection attacks that bypass memory score very differently, letting responders tell the attack types apart using tool-call logs alone.
